{{org}} identifies the data it holds whose confidentiality must survive beyond the next decade.
Certificate inventories record expiry and the algorithm in use, so a replacement can be planned rather than discovered.
ig2: The cryptographic inventory is produced as a machine-readable bill of materials rather than a hand-maintained document.
Vendors and service providers holding {{org}}'s data are asked, in writing, for their post-quantum migration plan.
Systems protecting long-lived confidential data are prioritized for migration, since their exposure begins before a quantum computer exists.
New designs record how the algorithm would be changed, and a design that cannot answer that is not approved.
ig3: {{org}} maintains a dated migration plan to the post-quantum standards, sequenced by data lifetime and system exposure.
Migration to a replacement algorithm is rehearsed on at least one production-representative system before it is required.
The cryptographic inventory is refreshed automatically and reconciled against the asset inventory at least {{review}}.

policies.exceptions: Continued use of a deprecated algorithm requires written approval from {{owner}}, a recorded reason, a compensating control, and a replacement date. The approval is time limited and does not renew automatically.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever a standards body deprecates an algorithm {{org}} relies on or publishes a new one.
evidence: The cryptographic inventory or bill of materials with its generation date
The list of deprecated algorithms in use and their replacement dates
Vendor responses on post-quantum readiness
The migration plan with sequencing and target dates

policies.title: Email and Web Protection Policy
policies.summary: Hardening the two channels most attacks arrive through.
policies.purpose: This policy sets the protections required on {{org}}'s email and web access, which are the most common initial access paths for attackers.
policies.scope: All email sent or received using {{org}}'s domains, and all web access from {{org}}'s managed devices and networks.

roles.responsibility: Sets the required email and web protections and reviews their effectiveness against reported phishing.
Configures and maintains mail authentication, filtering, and web protections.
Report suspected phishing through the provided mechanism rather than deleting it silently.

ig1: {{org}} publishes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for every domain it sends mail from.
Inbound mail is filtered for malicious content and known malicious senders.
Workers have a simple, always-available way to report a suspected phishing message.
Externally originated mail is visibly marked so recipients can tell it did not come from inside {{org}}.
Web access from managed devices is filtered against known malicious destinations.
Domains {{org}} owns but does not send mail from are configured so they cannot be used to send mail.
ig2: DMARC is set to a policy that instructs receivers to reject or quarantine failures, not merely to report them.
Reported phishing is triaged within a defined time, and confirmed messages are removed from other recipients' mailboxes.
Attachments and links are analyzed before delivery or on click, rather than trusted on sender reputation alone.
Mail forwarding rules to external addresses are restricted or alerted on, since they are a common exfiltration path.
Web filtering categories are reviewed so that the block list reflects {{org}}'s actual risk rather than defaults.
ig3: Phishing simulations are run at least {{review}}, and results drive targeted training rather than blame.
DMARC aggregate reports are monitored, so that abuse of {{org}}'s domains is detected.
Time from phishing report to removal from other mailboxes is measured and reported.
Detection exists for successful phishing, not only for attempted delivery.

policies.exceptions: A relaxation of these protections requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where email or web was the initial access path.
evidence: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records for all owned domains
The DMARC enforcement policy in effect
Phishing report triage times for the review period
Phishing simulation results and the training that followed

policies.title: Physical and Environmental Security Policy
policies.summary: Controlling who can physically reach systems and information, and protecting them from their environment.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} restricts physical access to its facilities, systems, and information, and protects them from environmental hazards.
policies.scope: All facilities {{org}} occupies, any equipment holding {{org}}'s information wherever it is located, and the working environments of remote workers to the extent {{org}} can set requirements.

appliesWhen.reason: Reduced scope: this organization operates no facilities of its own. Physical protection of equipment used by remote workers is covered by the Endpoint and Asset Management policies.

roles.responsibility: Sets physical security requirements for areas holding confidential information and reviews access records.
Administers physical access, maintains visitor records, and reports anomalies.
Do not admit unbadged individuals, secure their workspace, and protect equipment when working outside {{org}}'s facilities.

ig1: Physical access to areas holding systems or confidential information is restricted to authorized individuals.
Visitors to areas holding confidential information are recorded and accompanied.
Physical access is revoked on the same schedule as system access when a worker leaves.
Confidential information on paper is secured when unattended and disposed of by shredding or a secure disposal service.
Devices are not left unattended in public places, and screens are locked when the user steps away.
Equipment holding confidential information is protected from obvious environmental risks such as water and heat.
ig2: Physical access rights are reviewed at least {{review}}, and access that is no longer required is removed.
Physical access to areas holding confidential information is logged, and logs are retained for a defined period.
Deliveries and loading areas are separated from areas holding systems and confidential information.
Requirements for remote and home working are documented, covering how equipment and information are protected outside {{org}}'s facilities.
Server and network equipment areas have environmental protection appropriate to the value of what they hold.
ig3: Physical access logs are reviewed against expected activity, and anomalies are investigated.
Physical access controls to critical areas are tested rather than assumed effective.
Environmental monitoring alerts on conditions that threaten equipment before failure occurs.
Facilities holding the most sensitive information require more than one factor for physical entry.

policies.exceptions: Physical access arrangements departing from this policy require written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} changes premises or materially changes its remote working model.
evidence: Physical access authorization lists for restricted areas
Visitor records for the review period
The most recent physical access review
Secure disposal records for paper holding confidential information

policies.title: Secure Development Policy
policies.summary: Building security into software {{org}} writes, rather than testing for it at the end.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security requirements for software {{org}} develops or substantially customizes, so that defects are prevented and found early rather than discovered in production.
policies.scope: All software {{org}} writes, commissions, or materially customizes, including internal tools, infrastructure code, and scripts that handle confidential information.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization does not develop or materially customize software. If that changes, this policy becomes required.

roles.responsibility: Sets secure development requirements, reviews findings from testing, and advises on risk acceptance for unremediated defects.
Ensure their teams follow these requirements and that security findings are prioritized alongside functional work.
Write code to the standard, address findings in their own work, and never commit credentials to source control.

ig1: Source code is held in version control, and production changes are traceable to a commit and an author.
Credentials, keys, and tokens are never committed to source control, and repositories are scanned to enforce this.
Code changes are reviewed by someone other than the author before reaching production.
Third-party components are inventoried, and components with known vulnerabilities are updated.
Development and test environments do not use unmasked production data holding confidential information.
Developers receive secure development training relevant to the languages and platforms they use.
ig2: Automated security testing runs in the build pipeline, covering both first-party code and dependencies.
Findings above a defined severity block release, rather than being logged for later.
Applications handling confidential information are threat modeled before significant architectural change.
A software bill of materials is produced for applications {{org}} ships or operates in production.
Security requirements are defined at the start of a project rather than assessed at the end.
ig3: Applications handling confidential information are tested by an independent party at least {{review}}.
Build pipelines and artifact repositories are protected as production systems, since they can inject code into production.
Build provenance is recorded so that a deployed artifact can be traced to the source and process that produced it.
Defect escape rate and time to remediate are measured and reported.

policies.exceptions: Releasing with an unremediated finding above the blocking threshold requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented compensating control, and a remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a materially different development platform or delivery model.
evidence: Branch protection and code review settings
Security testing results from the build pipeline
Dependency inventory and its vulnerability status
Independent application test reports and remediation status

policies.title: API Security Policy
policies.summary: Inventory, authorization, and limits for the interfaces other software talks to.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} designs, publishes, authorizes, and retires its application programming interfaces, so that an interface built for one consumer does not become an unauthenticated path to everyone's data.
policies.scope: All APIs {{org}} exposes, whether public, partner-facing, or internal, and the APIs {{org}} consumes from third parties.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization does not develop or materially customize software, so it exposes no APIs of its own. If that changes, this policy becomes required.

roles.responsibility: Sets the API security standard, reviews the inventory for undocumented interfaces, and approves exceptions.
Register each API and version they operate, define who may call it, and retire versions rather than leaving them running.
Implement authorization at the object and function level, and never rely on the client to enforce what the server should.
Operate authentication, rate limiting, and logging at the gateway so controls do not have to be rebuilt per service.

ig1: {{org}} maintains an inventory of the APIs it exposes, including the version, the environment, and a named owner for each.
Every API requires authentication, and an unauthenticated endpoint exists only where public access is the documented purpose.
An API checks that the caller is authorized for the specific object requested, not merely that the caller is authenticated.
API requests and authorization failures are logged with enough detail to identify the caller.
Test, staging, and deprecated API versions are not left reachable from the internet.
ig2: APIs enforce rate limits and resource limits so that a single caller cannot exhaust the service for everyone else.
Input is validated against a defined schema, and responses return only the fields the caller is entitled to see.
API versions carry a published deprecation and retirement date, and retirement is executed on it.
Data received from a third-party API is treated as untrusted and validated before use.
ig3: APIs are tested for authorization flaws specifically, since scanners that look for injection will not find a broken object-level check.
Discovery runs against {{org}}'s external estate to find APIs that exist but were never registered.
Sensitive business flows are identified and protected against automated abuse, not only against malformed requests.

policies.exceptions: An API operating without authentication, authorization, or rate limiting requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, compensating monitoring, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} adopts a new API gateway or publishes a new class of external interface.
evidence: The API inventory with versions, environments, and owners
Gateway configuration showing authentication and rate limits in force
Authorization test results for a sample of endpoints
Deprecation notices and evidence of retired versions

policies.title: Software Assurance Maturity Policy
policies.summary: How security practice is built into how software is made, and how that is measured.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how security is embedded in {{org}}'s software development lifecycle and how consistently that practice is applied, so that secure development is a property of the process rather than of whichever engineer happened to be careful.
policies.scope: Every team that builds, customizes, or deploys software for {{org}}, and every stage from requirements through operation and decommissioning.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization does not develop or materially customize software. If that changes, this policy becomes required alongside the Secure Development Policy.

roles.responsibility: Defines the required security practices per lifecycle stage, measures adoption across teams, and reports maturity to leadership.
Owns adoption within their teams and funds the remediation of practice gaps rather than deferring them indefinitely.
Represent security inside a development team, run threat discussions, and escalate what the team cannot resolve.
Accept security requirements into the backlog on the same terms as functional requirements.

ig1: {{org}} names the maturity model its development practice is measured against and records the current level per practice.
Security requirements are written alongside functional requirements rather than added after a design is fixed.
Every development team knows which security practices are mandatory for it and where to find them.
Developers receive security training relevant to the languages and platforms they actually use.
Security findings are tracked in the same backlog as other defects, with the same visibility.
ig2: Each mandatory practice has a defined maturity target, and the distance to it is assessed at least {{review}}.
Threat modeling is performed for new services and for material changes to existing ones, and its output drives requirements.
Adoption of mandatory practices is measured per team rather than asserted for the organization as a whole.
A defect class that recurs across releases triggers a root cause review of the process, not another fix of the instance.
ig3: Maturity assessments are validated by someone outside the team being assessed.
The measured defect escape rate is used to judge whether a practice is working, and a practice that does not move it is changed.
Security practice requirements are applied to outsourced and contracted development on the same terms as to internal teams.

policies.exceptions: A team may operate below the mandatory practice set only with written approval from {{owner}} and engineering leadership, a recorded reason, and a dated plan to close the gap.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} materially changes its development toolchain or delivery model.
evidence: The maturity model in use and the current assessed level per practice
Per-team adoption measurement for mandatory practices
Threat models produced for new and materially changed services
Training completion records mapped to the technologies in use

policies.title: Change Management Policy
policies.summary: Changes are reviewed, recorded, and reversible, so that outages and weaknesses are not self-inflicted.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how changes to {{org}}'s systems are proposed, reviewed, approved, and recorded, so that change does not silently introduce risk or unavailability.
policies.scope: All changes to production systems, network and security configuration, access rights, and the pipelines that deploy them.

roles.responsibility: Ensures security implications are considered in change review and that emergency changes are reviewed afterwards.
Assess proposed changes for risk and impact, and approve or reject them before implementation.
Implement only approved changes, record what was done, and execute the rollback if the change fails.

ig1: Changes to production systems are recorded, including what changed, when, by whom, and why.
Changes are approved by someone other than the person implementing them before they reach production.
Changes carry a rollback plan, or a documented reason why rollback is not possible.
Emergency changes may bypass advance approval but are recorded and reviewed afterwards.
Changes to security controls, including firewall rules and access rights, follow this process.
Failed changes are recorded with their impact so that repeated failure modes become visible.
ig2: Change records are retained and can be reconciled against what actually changed in the environment.
Security review is required for changes affecting systems holding confidential information or controls that protect them.
Changes are tested in a non-production environment before production where the change type allows it.
Standard, low-risk changes are pre-approved through a documented definition rather than reviewed individually.
Emergency change volume is monitored, since a high rate usually indicates a process problem rather than genuine emergencies.
ig3: Detected configuration changes are reconciled against approved change records, and unmatched changes are investigated.
Change success and failure rates are measured and reported.
Automated controls prevent unapproved changes to critical production configuration.
Post-implementation review is required for changes above a defined risk threshold.

policies.exceptions: A change implemented outside this process requires retrospective approval from {{owner}} within a defined period, with the reason recorded.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident caused by an unmanaged or unreviewed change.
evidence: Change records for the review period, with approvals
Emergency change records and their retrospective reviews
Evidence of reconciliation between detected and approved changes
The definition of pre-approved standard changes

policies.title: Security Testing and Penetration Testing Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} has itself attacked on purpose, under a defined method, and acts on the result.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} commissions, scopes, authorizes, and acts on independent security testing, so that the organization learns what an attacker would find before an attacker finds it, and so that results can be compared from one year to the next.
policies.scope: All penetration testing, red team exercises, and adversary emulation performed against {{org}}'s systems, whether by internal staff or an external provider.

roles.responsibility: Commissions testing, approves scope and rules of engagement in writing, and owns the remediation of findings through to closure.
Authorizes testing against production systems and accepts the operational risk that authorization carries.
Remediate findings against their systems within the deadline the finding's severity sets, or request a documented exception.
Works to a named published methodology, stays inside the agreed scope, and reports findings with enough detail to reproduce them.

ig1: Independent security testing of internet-facing systems is performed at least {{review}}.
Every test is authorized in writing before it begins, with a defined scope, timing, and named contacts on both sides.
The test follows a named, published methodology so that its coverage is knowable rather than assumed.
Findings are recorded with a severity, a named owner, and a remediation deadline.
A finding is not closed until the fix has been verified, not merely reported as applied.
ig2: Rules of engagement state what testers may not do, how to stop a test, and how to distinguish a test from a real incident.
Testing covers internal systems and the paths available after an initial foothold, not only the external perimeter.
Retesting of remediated findings is included in the engagement rather than commissioned separately or skipped.
Test scope is reviewed against the current asset inventory so that new systems enter scope as they appear.
ig3: Adversary emulation exercises test detection and response, and the detection outcome is reported alongside the findings.
Testing is commissioned from a provider independent of the team that built or operates the systems under test.
Results are compared across engagements to show whether the same weakness classes keep returning.

policies.exceptions: Testing outside an approved scope is prohibited. A finding left unremediated past its deadline requires written risk acceptance from {{owner}}, a compensating control, and a revised date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after each engagement as part of its lessons learned.
evidence: Signed authorization and rules of engagement for each test
Test reports naming the methodology followed
Finding remediation records with verification evidence
Comparison of findings across successive engagements

policies.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance Policy
policies.summary: An inventory of AI use, an owner and risk tier for each, and a gate before it goes live.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} decides what artificial intelligence it will use, who is accountable for each use, what risk tier it falls into, and what review it must pass before it affects a real decision or a real person.
policies.scope: Every use of artificial intelligence in {{org}}'s work, whether built in house, bought as a product, embedded in a vendor's service, or adopted by a worker directly.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization records that it neither uses nor builds AI systems. In practice this is rare, since AI features arrive inside products already in use, which is what the discovery requirements in the Unsanctioned Technology policy exist to find.

roles.responsibility: Maintains the AI use case register, assigns the risk tier, and runs the review gate before a use case goes live.
Each AI use has a named accountable owner who answers for its outputs and for the decisions taken on them.
Determines which regulatory obligations attach to a use case and whether disclosure to affected people is required.
Approves the highest risk uses and the risk appetite that governs the tiering.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a register of its AI use cases, each with a named accountable owner and a description of what it is used for.
Every AI use case is assigned a risk tier before it goes live, and the tier determines the review it must pass.
Workers are told, in writing, which AI tools are approved and what categories of {{org}} data may be placed in each.
An AI output never becomes a decision about a person without a human who is accountable for that decision.
AI use that affects employment, credit, health, safety, or legal rights is escalated for review regardless of how routine it appears.
ig2: The register records, for each use case, what data it processes, what model or service it relies on, and what it is not approved to do.
A use case is reviewed again when its purpose, its data, or its underlying model materially changes.
Decisions taken with AI assistance in a high risk tier are documented well enough to be explained to the person affected.
Each use case names the conditions under which it would be suspended and who may suspend it.
ig3: High risk use cases carry a documented impact assessment covering affected people, failure modes, and the recourse available to them.
The register is reconciled at least {{review}} against discovery output, so undeclared AI use is found rather than assumed absent.
{{org}} reports its AI use and the risks it carries to leadership on the same cadence as other material risks.

policies.exceptions: An AI use case may not skip the review gate. Where a use is already live without one, it is registered, tiered, and reviewed within one cycle or withdrawn, with the decision recorded by {{owner}}.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever a regulatory obligation on AI takes effect in a jurisdiction {{org}} operates in.
evidence: The AI use case register with owners and risk tiers
Review gate records for use cases approved in the last cycle
The approved AI tool list and the data categories permitted in each
Impact assessments for high risk use cases

policies.title: AI Testing and Evaluation Policy
policies.summary: Measuring an AI system for accuracy, robustness, and abuse before and after it goes live.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} tests and evaluates the AI systems it builds or deploys, before release and on an ongoing basis, so that performance claims rest on measurement and degradation is detected rather than reported by a customer.
policies.scope: All AI and machine learning systems {{org}}, builds, fine tunes, or configures, including retrieval systems and prompt-based applications built on a third-party model.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization records that it does not build, tune, or deploy AI systems of its own. Where AI is consumed only as a vendor feature, the evaluation obligation sits with that vendor and is covered by the Third-Party and Supplier Security Policy.

roles.responsibility: Defines what must be measured before release, approves the acceptance thresholds, and can block a release that has not met them.
Define what correct performance means for their use case in terms someone outside the team can check.
Build and run the evaluation set, record results against each release, and report degradation rather than explaining it away.
Review outputs in their area of expertise, since accuracy against a benchmark is not the same as being right in context.

ig1: Every AI system has a written statement of what it is intended to do and what it is not intended to do.
An AI system is evaluated against a defined test set before it is released, and the result is recorded.
Acceptance thresholds are set before testing, not chosen afterward to match the result obtained.
A way for users to report a wrong or harmful output exists and is monitored.
Evaluation results are retained for each release, so performance can be compared across versions.
ig2: Evaluation covers robustness against adversarial and malformed input, not only accuracy on well-formed cases.
Systems that affect people are evaluated for disparate performance across the groups they affect.
Performance is monitored in production against the same measures used before release, and drift beyond the threshold raises an action.
The evaluation set is held separate from training and tuning data, and its integrity is protected.
ig3: High risk systems receive independent red teaming by testers who did not build the system.
Failure modes identified in evaluation are documented with the mitigations applied to each.
{{org}} can reproduce the evaluation result for any released version from its retained artifacts.

policies.exceptions: Releasing an AI system that has not met its acceptance thresholds requires written approval from {{owner}} and the use case owner, a documented limitation disclosed to users, and a fixed date for re-evaluation.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever a new class of AI system enters use that current evaluation methods do not cover.
evidence: Intended-use statements per AI system
Evaluation results and acceptance thresholds per release
Production monitoring output showing measured drift
Red team reports and the mitigations applied

policies.title: AI Model and Data Supply Chain Policy
policies.summary: Knowing where models, weights, and training data came from and whether they were tampered with.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} sources, verifies, and records the models, weights, datasets, and AI dependencies it relies on, so that a component obtained from a public repository cannot become an unexamined path into production.
policies.scope: All models, model weights, adapters, embeddings, datasets, prompt libraries, and AI-specific dependencies used in {{org}}'s systems, whether obtained commercially or from public sources.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization records that it does not build, tune, or deploy AI systems of its own, so it sources no models or datasets directly. If that changes, this policy becomes required.

roles.responsibility: Approves the sources models and datasets may be obtained from and reviews components that fall outside them.
Record the provenance of every model and dataset used, and verify integrity before a component reaches a build.
Confirm that data used for training or tuning may lawfully be used for that purpose and that its licensing permits it.
Obtains, from model and AI service providers, the same supply chain assurances required of any other supplier.

ig1: {{org}} records, for every model in use, where it came from, which version is deployed, and who approved it.
Models and datasets are obtained only from sources approved by {{owner}}.
Data used for training or tuning is confirmed to be lawfully usable for that purpose before it is used.
Model and dataset artifacts are stored in {{org}}'s own repository rather than pulled from a public source at deployment time.
AI-specific dependencies are covered by the same vulnerability management process as other software dependencies.
ig2: The integrity of a model artifact is verified against a published checksum or signature before it is used.
{{org}} maintains a bill of materials for its AI systems, listing models, datasets, and the dependencies beneath them.
Training and tuning data is version controlled, so the data behind a given model version can be identified.
A model or dataset withdrawn or found compromised upstream triggers an assessment of every system using it.
ig3: Model artifacts are cryptographically signed and signature verification is enforced at deployment.
Provenance records are sufficient to reconstruct which data contributed to a deployed model version.
Third-party model providers are assessed for their own supply chain controls, not only for their service availability.

policies.exceptions: Use of a model or dataset from an unapproved source requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented assessment of its provenance, isolation from production data, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} begins sourcing models or data from a new class of supplier.
evidence: The model and dataset register with provenance and approval records
The AI bill of materials for production systems
Integrity verification records for deployed model artifacts
Lawful basis and licensing confirmations for training data

policies.title: AI Application Security Policy
policies.summary: Guardrails on a live AI application: what goes in, what comes out, and what it may reach.
policies.purpose: This policy governs the controls {{org}} places around a running AI application, covering how untrusted input is handled, how output is treated before it is used, what data retrieval may reach, and what limits apply to consumption.
policies.scope: All AI applications {{org}} operates, including those built on third-party models, and the retrieval systems, vector stores, and plugins connected to them.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization records that it does not build, tune, or deploy AI systems of its own, so it operates no AI application runtime. If that changes, this policy becomes required.

roles.responsibility: Sets the required runtime controls per risk tier and approves any application that operates without one of them.
Implement the required controls, monitor their effectiveness, and report bypasses as security incidents.
Treat model output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it, and never pass it unchecked into a command, query, or rendered page.
Approve which of their data a retrieval system may index and confirm that retrieval respects the same permissions as direct access.

ig1: The system prompt and configuration of an AI application are treated as configuration to protect, not as a secret that provides security by itself.
Model output is validated and encoded before it is rendered, stored, or passed to another system.
An AI application reaches only the data its purpose requires, and that scope is written down.
Requests and responses are logged in a form that supports investigation, subject to the privacy policy's retention rules.
Usage limits are applied so that a single caller cannot exhaust capacity or run up unbounded cost.
ig2: Retrieval respects the requesting user's existing permissions, so an AI application cannot become a way to read what the user could not read directly.
Content that reaches the model from documents, web pages, or tool output is treated as untrusted instruction, not as trusted context.
Guardrails are applied to inputs and outputs for the categories of content the use case must not produce or accept.
Sensitive data is filtered or redacted before it reaches a third-party model endpoint.
ig3: Guardrail effectiveness is tested rather than assumed, and a bypass is treated as a security incident.
Anomalous usage patterns are detected and rate-limited automatically.
Vector stores and embeddings are protected and reviewed on the same terms as the source data they were derived from.

policies.exceptions: An AI application operating without a required runtime control needs written approval from {{owner}}, a compensating control, restricted data scope, and an expiry date no longer than one review cycle.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever a new attack technique against AI applications materially changes the required controls.
evidence: The required control set per risk tier and the implementation status per application
Retrieval permission model documentation
Guardrail test results including attempted bypasses
Usage and cost limit configuration

policies.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous Action Policy
policies.summary: What an AI agent may do on its own, under whose identity, and how a human stops it.
policies.purpose: This policy governs AI systems that take actions rather than only producing text, establishing what an agent may do without a human confirming each step, what identity it acts under, and how its activity is traced and stopped.
policies.scope: All AI agents operating in {{org}}'s environment, including those that call tools, invoke APIs, write to systems, spend money, or coordinate with other agents.

appliesWhen.reason: Not applicable: this organization records that it does not build, tune, or deploy AI systems of its own, so it operates no agents. If that changes, this policy becomes required before an agent is given any ability to act.

roles.responsibility: Approves what each agent may do autonomously, sets the actions that always require a human, and can revoke an agent's access immediately.
Each agent has a named human owner accountable for what it does, who reviews its activity and answers for its actions.
Grant each agent its own identity and the narrowest tool permissions that let it work, and build the stop mechanism before the agent is deployed.
Approve, for their own system, whether an agent may act on it and under what constraints.

ig1: Every agent has a named human owner who is accountable for the actions it takes.
An agent acts under its own distinct identity, never under a person's credentials or a shared administrative account.
Actions that are irreversible, that spend money, that change access, or that affect a person require human confirmation before they proceed.
Every action an agent takes is logged with the agent's identity, the action, and the input that prompted it.
A documented way to stop an agent immediately exists and is known to the people who may need to use it.
ig2: An agent receives only the tools and permissions its task requires, and a new tool is added only with the owner's approval.
An agent's working memory and instruction sources are protected, since content it reads can become instruction it follows.
Agent activity is bounded by limits on time, spend, and number of actions, and exceeding a limit stops the agent rather than continuing.
Where agents communicate with each other, the trust between them is explicit, and one agent's output is not treated as authoritative instruction by another.
ig3: Agent behavior is monitored against its expected pattern, and deviation triggers suspension pending review.
The volume of confirmations put to a human is measured and controlled, since a person asked to approve everything approves without reading.
Agent permissions are reviewed at least {{review}} on the same terms as privileged human access.

policies.exceptions: Granting an agent autonomous ability to take an action this policy requires a human to confirm needs written approval from {{owner}}, the system owner, a bounded scope, additional monitoring, and an expiry date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever an agent is given a materially broader ability to act.
evidence: The agent register with owners, identities, and approved tool permissions
Action logs showing agent identity and the human confirmations obtained
Documented stop procedures and evidence they have been tested
The most recent review of agent permissions

policies.title: Logging, Monitoring, and Detection Policy
policies.summary: Collecting the evidence needed to notice an incident and to reconstruct it afterwards.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes what {{org}} logs, how long it keeps logs, and how those logs are monitored, so that security events can be detected and investigated.
policies.scope: All systems, applications, and services {{org}} operates or subscribes to that process confidential information or control access to it.

roles.responsibility: Defines what must be logged, sets retention, and reviews whether detection coverage matches {{org}}'s risks.
Ensure their systems produce the required logs and forward them to the central store.
Maintains log collection, monitors for gaps in ingestion, and preserves logs against alteration.

ig1: Authentication successes and failures, and administrative actions, are logged on systems holding confidential information.
Logs are retained for a documented minimum period sufficient to investigate an incident discovered late.
System clocks are synchronized to a common time source so that events across systems can be correlated.
Logs are stored so that the account generating an event cannot alter or delete the record of it.
A named individual is responsible for reviewing security-relevant events on a defined cadence.
Loss of logging from a system in scope is itself treated as an event to investigate.
ig2: Logs from systems holding confidential information are forwarded to a central store separate from the systems that produce them.
Detection rules exist for the events {{org}} has decided matter, and each rule has a documented response.
Alerts are routed to a person or team accountable for triaging them within a defined time.
Log coverage is reconciled against the asset inventory so that systems silently not logging are found.
Retention meets the longest applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, not merely operational convenience.
ig3: Detection coverage is mapped against a recognized adversary technique catalogue, and gaps are tracked.
Detection rules are tested by simulating the activity they are meant to catch.
Time from event to alert and from alert to triage is measured and reported.
Log integrity is verifiable, so that evidence would withstand challenge.

policies.exceptions: A system in scope that cannot produce required logs may operate only with written approval from {{owner}}, a compensating detective control, and a documented remediation date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where insufficient logging hindered investigation.
evidence: The logging standard stating what must be logged and for how long
Log coverage reconciled against the asset inventory
Detection rules and their documented responses
Alert triage records showing time to response

policies.title: Incident Response Policy
policies.summary: How {{org}} detects, declares, contains, and learns from security incidents, and who decides what.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} prepares for and responds to security incidents, so that response is decided in advance rather than improvised under pressure.
policies.scope: Any event that compromises, or credibly threatens to compromise, the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of {{org}}'s information or systems, including events at a supplier that affect {{org}}.

roles.responsibility: Runs the response, makes containment decisions, and is the single point of coordination for the duration of an incident.
Maintains this policy and the response plan, and appoints the incident commander for each incident.
Decides on external notification, regulatory reporting, and any payment or legal action.
Report suspected incidents immediately and preserve evidence rather than attempting to remediate alone.

ig1: {{org}} maintains a written incident response plan that names who to contact, in what order, at any hour.
Every worker knows how to report a suspected incident, and reporting is possible without going through the worker's own manager.
Incidents are recorded with what happened, when it was detected, what was done, and who decided.
A named individual has authority to declare an incident and to take systems offline to contain it.
{{org}} knows which regulators, customers, or insurers it may be obliged to notify, and within what deadline, before an incident occurs.
Contact details for law enforcement, legal counsel, and any cyber insurer are recorded and reachable outside normal business hours.
After a significant incident, {{org}} performs a review and records what will change as a result.
ig2: The incident response plan is tested at least {{review}} through a tabletop or live exercise, and the plan is updated with what the exercise found.
Incidents are classified by severity using documented criteria, and severity drives escalation and notification timing.
{{org}} maintains the ability to preserve logs and forensic evidence before remediating, where doing so does not prolong material harm.
Response roles have named alternates, so a single person's absence does not stall the response.
Third-party incidents affecting {{org}} are handled under this policy, and supplier contracts require prompt notification.
ig3: {{org}} measures and reports mean time to detect and mean time to contain, and treats adverse trends as findings.
Post-incident actions are tracked to closure with named owners and dates, and closure is verified rather than asserted.
Exercises include at least one scenario per year that assumes a control failed rather than held.
An external party is retained in advance for forensic support, so engagement does not begin during an incident.

policies.exceptions: Deviation from the response plan during an active incident is permitted where the incident commander judges it necessary, and must be recorded in the incident log and reviewed afterwards.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, after any significant incident, and after any exercise that identifies a gap.
evidence: The current incident response plan, with version and approval date
Incident records for the review period
Exercise records, including what changed as a result
Post-incident review findings and their closure status

policies.title: Backup and Recovery Policy
policies.summary: Copies that survive the event that destroyed the original, and that are proven to restore.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} backs up its information and validates that it can be restored, so that recovery is a tested capability rather than an assumption.
policies.scope: All systems and information required to operate {{org}}, including data held in cloud services where the provider does not guarantee recovery to {{org}}'s requirements.

roles.responsibility: Sets backup and retention requirements based on recovery objectives and reviews restore test results.
Define the recovery point and recovery time objectives their system requires and confirm backups meet them.
Runs backups, monitors for failures, and performs restore testing on schedule.

ig1: Systems and information required to operate {{org}} are backed up on a defined schedule.
At least one backup copy is held offline, off-site, or in an account separate from the systems it protects.
Backups of confidential information are encrypted.
Backup failures generate an alert to a named owner rather than failing silently.
A restore is tested at least {{review}}, and the test is recorded with its outcome.
Access to backups and to backup configuration is restricted to a small, documented set of accounts.
ig2: Recovery point and recovery time objectives are documented per system and backup schedules are set to meet them.
Backup copies are protected against deletion or encryption by an attacker who has compromised production credentials.
Restore testing covers full system recovery, not only individual file restoration.
Data held in cloud services is backed up where the provider's native retention does not meet {{org}}'s objectives.
Backup retention meets the longest applicable regulatory or contractual obligation.
ig3: Restore testing is performed against the documented recovery time objective, and shortfalls are treated as findings.
At least one backup copy is immutable for a defined period.
Recovery is exercised as part of incident response testing, using the backups that would actually be used.
Backup integrity is verified rather than inferred from job success.

policies.exceptions: A system operating without backups meeting this policy requires written approval from {{owner}}, an accepted recovery risk recorded in the risk register, and a review date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever recovery objectives change or a restore test fails to meet them.
evidence: Backup schedules and their coverage against critical systems
Restore test records with dates and outcomes
Evidence that a copy is isolated from production credentials
Documented recovery objectives per system

policies.title: Business Continuity Policy
policies.summary: Keeping {{org}} running through disruption, and knowing in advance what has to come back first.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes how {{org}} prepares to continue operating through significant disruption, and how it decides what to restore first.
policies.scope: All business processes {{org}} depends on and the systems, people, facilities, and suppliers that support them.

roles.responsibility: Approves recovery priorities and the level of disruption {{org}} is prepared to accept.
Maintains this policy and coordinates continuity planning and exercises across the business.
Identify what their process requires to operate and document how it would run in degraded conditions.

ig1: {{org}} has identified the business processes it cannot operate without and the systems each one depends on.
Recovery priorities are documented and approved by leadership before an event, not decided during one.
Continuity and recovery plans record who does what, and are reachable when normal systems are unavailable.
Contact details for staff, key suppliers, and customers are maintained and accessible outside primary systems.
Plans state how the business would operate manually or in degraded mode where that is possible.
Plans are reviewed at least {{review}} and after any material change to the business.
ig2: A business impact analysis is performed at least {{review}}, quantifying the impact of losing each critical process over time.
Recovery time and recovery point objectives are set per process from that analysis, and systems are provisioned to meet them.
Continuity plans are exercised at least {{review}}, and findings are tracked to closure.
Dependencies on single suppliers or single locations for critical processes are documented and escalated to leadership.
Plans cover loss of key personnel, not only loss of systems or facilities.
ig3: Exercises include scenarios where the primary recovery option is unavailable.
Achieved recovery times from exercises are compared to objectives, and shortfalls are treated as findings.
Continuity arrangements with critical suppliers are validated rather than accepted on assertion.
Continuity requirements are considered before adopting a new critical system or supplier.

policies.exceptions: Operating a critical process without a documented continuity plan requires written approval from leadership, an accepted risk recorded in the risk register, and a date by which a plan will exist.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, after any significant disruption, and after any exercise that identifies a material gap.
evidence: The list of critical processes and their dependencies
The most recent business impact analysis
Exercise records and the findings they produced
Documented recovery objectives approved by leadership

policies.title: Security Awareness and Training Policy
policies.summary: Making sure people know what is expected of them, in terms relevant to their actual job.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security training {{org}} provides, so that workers understand the risks relevant to their role and what they are expected to do about them.
policies.scope: All workers and contractors with access to {{org}}'s information or systems, including those in roles with elevated privileges or specialized responsibilities.

roles.responsibility: Defines the training programme, keeps content current with the threats {{org}} actually faces, and reports completion.
Enrolls new joiners before or on their start date and tracks completion as a condition of continued access.
Ensure their teams complete required training and reinforce expectations in day-to-day work.

ig1: Every worker completes security awareness training on joining and at least {{review}} thereafter.
Training covers how to recognize and report phishing, how to handle confidential information, and how to report an incident.
Completion is tracked, and non-completion is escalated rather than ignored.
Workers are told which behaviours are prohibited and what the consequences of violation are.
Training content is reviewed at least {{review}} so that it reflects current threats rather than last decade's.
New joiners acknowledge {{org}}'s security policies as part of onboarding.
ig2: Roles with elevated risk receive additional training specific to their responsibilities, such as developers and administrators.
Phishing simulation results inform who receives targeted follow-up training.
Training includes {{org}}'s own incident reporting route and named contacts, not generic advice.
Workers handling regulated information receive training on the specific obligations that attach to it.
Awareness activity happens between annual training, rather than only once a year.
ig3: Training effectiveness is measured through behaviour, such as reporting rates and simulation outcomes, not completion alone.
Leadership and those with authority to approve payments or access receive training on the attacks that target them specifically.
Security expectations are included in role descriptions and performance conversations for roles with security responsibilities.
The programme is adjusted based on the incidents and near misses {{org}} actually experiences.

policies.exceptions: A worker may retain access without current training only with written approval from {{owner}}, for a stated period, and with a completion date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and after any incident where a lack of awareness was a contributing factor.
evidence: Training completion records for the review period
The current training content and its last review date
Phishing simulation results and follow-up training records
Onboarding records showing policy acknowledgement

policies.title: Personnel Security Policy
policies.summary: Security obligations across the employment lifecycle, from screening to the day someone leaves.
policies.purpose: This policy establishes the security requirements that apply to workers before, during, and after their engagement with {{org}}.
policies.scope: All employees, contractors, and temporary workers, and any third-party personnel granted access to {{org}}'s information or systems.

roles.responsibility: Runs screening, ensures agreements are signed, and notifies system owners of joiners, movers, and leavers in time to act.
Defines screening requirements proportionate to role risk and confirms access removal on departure.
Confirm what access their reports require, and initiate the leaver process promptly including for involuntary departures.

ig1: Workers accept written confidentiality obligations before being granted access to confidential information.
Workers acknowledge {{org}}'s security policies on joining.
A documented leaver process removes system access, recovers equipment, and revokes physical access.
Managers notify people operations and IT of departures with enough notice for access to be removed on the final day.
Involuntary departures trigger immediate access removal, coordinated with the departure itself.
Confidentiality obligations continue after the engagement ends, and workers are reminded of this on departure.
ig2: Background screening proportionate to role risk is completed before access to confidential information is granted.
Role changes trigger an access review, so that permissions accumulated in a previous role are removed.
Contractors and third-party personnel are subject to equivalent requirements, evidenced through their employer where {{org}} does not screen directly.
Security responsibilities are stated in role descriptions for roles that carry them.
Departure checklists are completed and retained, rather than assumed done.
ig3: Screening for roles with the highest access is repeated on a defined cycle rather than only at hire.
Access removal on departure is verified against the account inventory rather than assumed from the checklist.
Departures of workers with privileged access trigger a review of their recent activity.
Time from departure to complete access removal is measured and reported.

policies.exceptions: Granting access before screening or agreements are complete requires written approval from {{owner}}, a documented reason, and a completion date.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever {{org}} materially changes how it engages workers.
evidence: Signed confidentiality agreements and policy acknowledgements
Screening records appropriate to role risk
Completed leaver checklists with access removal timing
Evidence of access review following role changes

policies.title: Security Workforce and Skills Policy
policies.summary: The security work roles {{org}} needs, the skills each requires, and how people grow into them.
policies.purpose: This policy governs how {{org}} defines the security work its program requires, the skills each role needs, and how it hires, develops, and retains the people to do it, so that a capability gap is identified as a planning problem rather than discovered during an incident.
policies.scope: All roles with security responsibility at {{org}}, whether in a dedicated security function, embedded in another team, or delivered by a contracted provider.

roles.responsibility: Defines the security work roles required, assesses the skills held against them, and reports capability gaps to leadership.
Writes role descriptions against the defined work roles and supports development plans and retention for security staff.
Recruit against the defined skills for the role rather than against a list of certifications, and identify gaps a hire will not close.
Funds the staffing and development the assessed gaps require, or accepts in writing the risk of leaving them open.

ig1: {{org}} names the security work its program requires and who performs each part, including work delivered by a provider.
Security responsibilities are written into the role descriptions of the people who hold them.
Critical security tasks have a documented backup, so a single person's absence does not stop the work.
Workers performing security work receive training relevant to the tasks they actually perform.
Capability gaps are recorded and reported to leadership rather than absorbed quietly by the people covering them.
ig2: Roles are defined against a published workforce framework, so skills can be described consistently rather than invented per posting.
Skills held are assessed against skills required at least {{review}}, and the gap drives hiring and development decisions.
Each person doing security work has a development plan tied to the skills their role requires.
Where a capability is bought from a provider, the skills that provider must hold are stated in the contract.
ig3: Succession is planned for the roles whose loss would materially disrupt the security program.
Capability is measured through exercises and practical assessment rather than through training completion alone.
Workforce planning is projected against the program roadmap, so the skills for planned work are secured before the work starts.

policies.exceptions: A security work role left unfilled or a critical task left without a backup requires written acknowledgement from {{owner}} and executive leadership, a compensating arrangement, and a date for resolution.
policies.review: This policy is reviewed {{review}}, and whenever the security program takes on a class of work the current roles do not cover.
evidence: The defined security work roles and who holds each
The most recent skills assessment against required skills
Development plans for staff performing security work
Capability gap reporting delivered to leadership
